inline.s: A bright moon trails her shadow down the heavenly street; drunk in the east wind, I lean alone upon the rail. When court is done and the ninefold palace falls to silence, the six palaces still array their caps and gowns.

Master Luzu, whenever he saw a monk approach, would simply turn and face the wall. When Nanquan heard of this he said, “I am always telling monks and teachers: grasp it before the Buddha ever appeared in the world — and still you do not get one half of one. If he carries on like that, he will wait till the year of the donkey, a year that never comes.” The gāthā says:

Beneath the snow on the cold cliff lies one branch of plum; its boundless spring light it will not open wide. Yet the east wind lightly lets the secret slip, and hidden fragrance drifts into my dream.

Weishan addressed the assembly, saying, “A hundred years from now I shall be a water buffalo down the mountain. On its left flank five words shall be written: The monk of Weishan, so-and-so. Then if you call it the monk of Weishan, it is a water buffalo; if you call it a water buffalo, it is the monk of Weishan. What, then, will you call it?” The gāthā says:

In the belly of a horse, in the womb of an ass, lies the house of buddhas and patriarchs; where the great man walks, the road stretches far. If the water buffalo is measured against old Weishan, its horns stand high — and still it yields to him.
A monk asked Yunmen, “What is Buddha?” Yunmen said, “A dried shit-stick.” The gāthā says:

Mountains, rivers and lands stand openly revealed; rubble and thickets all give forth their light. But let a single mote of dust stand before your face, and buddhas countless as the Ganges sands are hidden quite.
Gāthās on the Diamond Sūtra (Eighteen Poems)
The World-Honored One Puts On His Robe and Takes Up His Bowl; Subhūti Sighs That This Is Rare
To put on the robe and take the bowl is just like this; to eat and walk in mindfulness — what is so wondrous there? Why then did Subhūti sigh that it was rare, leaving people all the more perplexed?
Thus Should One Abide
At the road's end, cold looks and desolation; then all at once you meet the great resting place. Let go, and this becomes the land of peace — why trouble yourself with grief and long debate?
Thus Should One Subdue the Mind

On the wall the lamplight plays at children's shapes; in the black night you suspect a ghost is at your heels. Wait for daybreak and see through it for yourself — all that alarm and delight, to whom will you tell it?
In Truth Not One Being Attains Deliverance

Last night I dreamed I came to the Ghost Gate Pass; countless rākṣasas thronged the Iron Mountain round. The cold cock crowed, the sky broke into dawn — I turned, and one smile scattered all my grief.
Not Abiding in Marks
A gandharva city fallen into a mirror; towers and halls and pavilions fill the void. Only look at the countless visitors who climb there, leaning on the rail, robes thrown open, seeing off the geese.
Giving Rise to the Mind That Dwells Nowhere

Seek not at random the tracks of birds and fish; lightning and flint-spark allow the mind no room. People today hear only the clamor of spring birds — who believes the note within the kalavinka's egg?
No Self, No Person, No Being, No Life-Span

The puppets mount the stage and wait for drum and gong; everyone gathers round to hear the loud song. You do not know whose hand the strings are in; when the strings snap, what shame and confusion follow.
The Four Fruits Form No Such Thought

A wayside inn on a long road, briefly welcoming travellers; one night of rest — how could it last? In a dream I suddenly climbed to the Tuṣita heaven; turning my head, all that fine thinking was spent for nothing.
Before Dīpaṃkara Buddha, in Truth Nothing Was Attained

Young, I took up book and sword and went to a far country, meaning in time to enter the examination hall. By chance in the street I met a diviner, who told me I should be the topmost scholar of them all.
To Hold Four Lines of Verse Brings Blessings Great

Year after year ghosts haunt us and shamans are called in; driven off, they come again and leave their filth behind. By the statute of the Most High Lord Lao, from this day let all evil spirits be driven away together.
Subhūti Is Moved to Tears

Who knows the place where the heart aches? A kingdom in mourning, a family ruined — and to whom shall I speak? I turn my head; from my old home no word comes. I cannot bear to hear the wild goose's grief again.
King Kali Cuts His Body Limb from Limb
King Mu loved the man made by Yanshi; the singing and laughter seemed so truly real. One burst of anger and it was torn apart — only then did he know it was glued and lacquered into a body.
A Single Thought of Faith Attains Bodhi

Say not the dog-butcher was unworthy of the Yi Gate's recommendation; one word of promise and he pledged his golden self. Hammer in hand, he walked straight into the commander's tent and seized the tally from the general's elbow.
The Three Minds Cannot Be Attained

Through the cold, vast sky a lone wild goose journeys on; the straining eye grows dim and miles are heaped on miles. Its traces were cut off from the very beginning — I urge you, do not reckon up the road.
There Is No Dharma That Can Be Spoken
In the house of illusions the tricks are many; the singing never stops, the dancers whirl. Pity the watchers, who only add to their grief and joy — have you ever seen the single thread behind it all?
The Tathāgata Says They Are Not Beings; Therefore They Are Called Beings

The painter follows his fancy, drawing forms and faces; features, robes and caps all differ one from another. Fair or foul, let him sort them all he likes — in the end not one of them is the true master.
The Tathāgata Says the Ordinary Being Is Not an Ordinary Being

High and low were never fixed by any rule; from a white-walled cottage ministers have always come. Once the Son of Heaven proclaims the edict in person, you are there and then the first name on the list.
The Tathāgata Comes from Nowhere and Goes Nowhere
I dreamed I wandered in the land of Huaxu; joyful on arriving, sorrowful on turning back. One cock-crow and the frosty sky grows light — empty flowers fall from my pillow into both eyes.
Gāthās on the Sixteen Sublime Contemplations of the Pure Land
1. The First, the Sun Contemplation: Behold the Setting Sun as a Hanging Drum
The white sun sinks in the west, and there I lodge my longing; where the sunset ends, the mind knows. Since we parted no word has come — and yet from then on it is ever as if we were face to face.
2. The Second, the Water Contemplation: Behold the Great Waters Clear and Still, Frozen to Ice and Radiant; Form the Perception of Vaiḍūrya
The cool mind-ground, blue and crystalline; translucent as water turned to ice. One shining field of pure vaiḍūrya — let it not bury the old barbarian monk.
3. The Third, the Ground Contemplation: Behold Ice and Vaiḍūrya; Accomplish the Perception of the Ground
Where can the roaming mind walk? The jewelled ground of vaiḍūrya is level as a palm. Before the foot moves, the step ahead is already taken — and yet it never travelled any road at all.
4. The Fourth, the Tree Contemplation: On the Vaiḍūrya Ground, Form the Perception of Jewelled Trees

Row upon row of trees, a forest of the seven jewels; arrayed before the eyes, solemn and deep in shade. The flowers hold countless maṇi gems within; when the wind stirs, they ever proclaim the wondrous Dharma sound.
5. The Fifth, the Pool Contemplation: In the Seven-Jewelled Pools, Form the Perception of the Water of Eight Good Qualities

The king of wish-fulfilling pearls wells up as a spring; the water holds eight virtues and flows among the flowers. On the diamond pool's floor the golden sand is spread; thought after thought the seven-jewelled lotus opens in the mind.
6. The Sixth, the Comprehensive Contemplation: Form the Perception of Jewelled Pavilions
Jewelled and adorned, the pavilions rise in tier on tier; countless devas assemble within. Unstruck, the heavenly music sounds of itself; the Dharma fills the ear and the joy is without end.
7. The Seventh, the Seat Contemplation: Within the Seven-Jewelled Lotus, Form the Perception of the Diamond Throne
The seven-jewelled flower holds a seven-jewelled throne; maṇi stamens and pistils knit the womb. As the mind wills, one field of radiant light — and one's own golden form appears therein.
8. The Eighth, the Image Contemplation: Form the Perception of One Buddha and Two Bodhisattvas

Marks and excellences, radiance, a body like water and moon — just as a lost child sees his kind mother again. From today, once you know the face you had before your mother bore you, you will no longer be a wanderer on the long road.
9. The Ninth, the Buddha Contemplation: Form the Perception of the Buddha's Marks and Excellences

The white-hair curl is Sumeru, the eyes are lotuses; mark upon mark of excellence, all without bound. Every pore of the whole body gathers light, illumining the three thousand and the great thousand worlds.
10. The Tenth, the Contemplation of Avalokiteśvara: Form the Image of the Great Being, with a Buddha Standing in His Crown

The great being's body, vast and without bound; in the light of his crown, transformed buddhas numberless as dust. Look closely: in each pore lie the lands of living beings; whatever meets the eye is clearly an old friend.
11. The Eleventh, the Contemplation of Mahāsthāmaprāpta: Form the Perception of Him Seated Upright, Holding a Lotus

Light, form and feature are all without fault; on his head a heavenly crown of a hundred jewelled flowers. Within those flowers pure buddha-lands are held — and no one knows who the master of the house may be.
12. The Twelfth, the Universal Contemplation: Form the Perception of Oneself Reborn, with the Lotus Opening and Closing
The mind conceives a lotus vast as space; reborn deep within, in a secrecy none may pierce. When the light shines through and the flower opens — waking eyes still find it like a dream.
13. The Thirteenth, the Miscellaneous Contemplation: Form the Perception of the Buddha in Bodies Great and Small, Not Fixed

A hundred rivers hold the moon, its shadows uneven; it goes and comes with each person, wherever he may go. You would say the two ends make two separate roads — who knows that in all its moving it never moved?
14. The Fourteenth, the Contemplation of the Three Highest Grades
The mind imagines climbing far to the Tuṣita palace; adorned and wondrous, realm upon realm. I hear Maitreya speak the truth myself — only I fear the meeting is a dream.
15. The Fifteenth, the Contemplation of the Three Middle Grades

The Son of Heaven seeks talent, choosing the filial and upright; village verdicts, great and small, all call them worthy. One day they climb the golden hall by special grace — that a white-walled cottage yields a minister is no accident.
16. The Sixteenth, the Contemplation of the Three Lowest Grades

Sword-trees and knife-mountains stand before the eyes; one turn of the light, and they become golden lotuses. To rise to general from a grave-robber is a hero's deed; only then you believe that office is not bought with coin.
A Gāthā on the Dharma of Original Abiding, in Celebration of the Eightieth Year of Chan Master Wunian of Mount Huangbo (with Preface)

In the third year of His Majesty's reign, in mid-spring of the guihai year, on the seventeenth day of the second month, fell the day of the four hundred and eightieth jiazi of Chan Master Wunian of Mount Huangbo. From his youth the Master set his will on the highest; he awakened early to his own mind, opened the true eye upon his brow, and raised the banner of fearlessness. The Dharma gate looks to him with reverence, and monks flock to him like the wind; all are guided to the supreme meaning and brought to enter the ground of self-confidence. Truly he is a ford and bridge in the age of the Dharma's decline, a torch of wisdom in the long night. The Chan school has fallen into decline, and it is owing to the Master alone that its family voice is still sounded. I, unwise as I am, have never beheld his countenance, yet the light of our minds shines upon each other with not a hair's breadth between. In the Dharma we forget feeling and hold no mark of self or other — and this has been so for many a day. Alas, I am old now, and I am ashamed that I cannot once take up the fly-whisk with him to seal a bond of Dharma joy. Now, happily, I meet the day of the Master's manifestation in birth; officials and laymen of the ten directions, black-robed and white-robed alike, each bring offerings and raise their praise. Hearing of it, I rejoice, and say to myself: one who awakens to the unborn is free of the mark of a life-span and cannot be moved by the four marks — how could one measure him by worldly truth? So I speak a gāthā on the Dharma of Original Abiding, and respectfully send an attendant to carry incense and flowers afar, to express my praise. It is to measure the great ocean with a drop of water, to view the vast void through a crack; I would not presume to exhaust his bounds, but only to show a little of my sincerity, in the spirit of offering the Dharma. And the gāthā says:

The self-nature of all dharmas is ever quiescent and extinguished, still and unmoving as empty space. The world's dense array and all its myriad forms are sealed by this one Dharma alone. Before the Buddha appeared, before the patriarchs came, this Dharma of original abiding lacked nothing. Blades of grass and motes of dust have their essence complete; even the white ox and the dark slave know it is there. How much more do living beings, each fully endowed, share a nature equal with all buddhas. This equal self-nature knows no birth or death — how could the four marks ever move it? It neither comes nor goes, has no beginning or end; therefore it is called the Dharma of original abiding. If one awakens to this and embodies suchness, in one leap he cuts off the views of ordinary being and sage. When the true eye opens, birth and death are empty; the two gates of delusion and awakening fly open on the spot. One who has passed the gate swings his arms and walks, treading the great square alone with no hindrance, like a lion roaming at ease — no jackal may follow in his tracks. He tears away the thatch that seals the five aggregates and sits openly on bare ground, robe thrown back, at peace. This is called the fearless, liberated one; from then on he ever abides in this Dharma. It is the Master alone who has understood this Dharma of original abiding, sitting alone on Huangbo's highest peak, lofty and unmoved as Sumeru, while all the myriad forms bow their heads to him. Sun and moon move on like flashes of lightning; the world's mountains and rivers are shadows in a mirror. Indeed, since mind is empty, body too is empty, blending all dharmas with no rising or ceasing. Thus one mote of dust joined with emptiness becomes one body with all space, and so with every mote of dust: body and dust are equal, not two. Once body and dust enter the emptiness of the Dharma realm, the essence of self-nature equals space. This emptiness is itself the Dharma of original abiding; one who enters it has a life without measure. Within space, worlds may rise and cease as they will; all sages and ordinary beings come and go. This Dharma is unmoved, its mark ever abiding; it is the life-span of all beings on earth. Since living beings are one with all buddhas, how could my Master differ from living beings? May my Master ever manifest and be born among them, realizing and entering the measureless life of all beings.
A Seat-Side Admonition, Shown to Master Huang

Desire must not be indulged; the will must not be unsettled; the nature must not turn perverse; the mind must not run loose; the body must not grow slack; learning must not be shallow; principle must not be obscured; thought must not be wild. Do not let idleness carry you outward; do not let craving destroy you within. Dwell in calm and quiet, and all your limbs will come to no harm; be not seduced by things, and your spirit will be king of itself.
An Admonition on Settling the Will, Shown to Master Jiang

Be not restless in the mire of worldly desire; be not sullen in disordered thought; be not proud as a floating cloud; be not chasing after the nets of the world. Rather, settle your will and dwell in simplicity; seek to gather your spirit and nourish it in stillness. Feed on wild greens with contentment; enjoy clear hills and waters alone. Open the Dark and the Changes to fathom transformation; read the Spring and Autumn Annals to mirror the past. Recite the Nanhua to dissolve your cares; knock at the Western scriptures to break through your hindrances. See the world's ways as a heat-haze; hear praise and blame as echoes in a valley. Look on all things as a worm's arm; regard this body as a rat's burrow. What do riches and honor ask of me? Gain and loss in others' hands turn like a palm. Bright before you, shining above you — be not reckless, be not scheming: what confusion, what blur? In form like a wooden cock, in mind like Xiangwang, blank and unknowing. Confucius said, “Free from envy, free from greed — what course could fail to be good?” This is what is called excellence enduring.
The Admonition on Self

All love and hate arise from the hindrance of self. If the hindrance of self is emptied, the light is measureless. When mind arises chasing objects, when thought stirs following feeling — forget both mind and object, and things and self are undivided. Things have no beauty or ugliness; it is the self that makes them right or wrong. If my mind does not arise, what can those things do? View motion and stillness as equal; see high and low as one; level ordinary beings and sages alike — this is called the inconceivable.
The Admonition on the Body

Reverently I ask you, body: what are you? A compound of the four elements, false within and without — gathered foam, a plantain trunk, dust and heat-haze; a dense forest of many sufferings, a vast wilderness of birth and death. Many are blind to it; few understand. When one breath fails to come, you are a wen, a clod of earth.
The Admonition on the Mind

What are you, mind — dim and unfathomable? You are the norm of things, the spirit of man; bright and undimmed, clear and ever awake. You are the storehouse of good and evil, the court of sages and saints. Let not desire obscure you; let not delusion entangle you. In calm and quiet, your spirit finds its own peace.
The Admonition on the Nature

Your essence is perfect and bright, your form subtle and profound; unmoved and unchanging, without mark or feature — as water is wet, as fire is dry. Through all transformation it does not shift; words and names cannot reach it. Gone or abiding, coming or now; at leisure or busy, still or restless — it stands alone, and this is called the true Way.
The Admonition on Destiny

I ask you, whence do you come? Truly by Heaven's favor. Long life or early death, poverty or success — let them come as they will. Be not envious, not greedy; bear no grudge, no hatred. Dwell like a quail, eat like a fledgling; be dragon-cloud or leopard-mist. Trust your spirit: rise and fall have their number. Be at peace and wait, and allow no longing for what lies outside.
An Inscription on Mother and Son (with Preface)

Because he spread the Dharma, Qing brought trouble upon himself and provoked the anger of the sage Son of Heaven; the voice of it was like thunder. Privately I thought of my old mother: hearing it, she would surely be frightened out of her wits. Yet by grace I was spared from death and sent into exile at Leiyang. Passing through my native place, I welcomed my old mother on the river. At the first sight of me she laughed and talked, her voice clear and bright, with not the slightest tangled thought in her breast. So I asked her, “Mother, when you heard that your son stood between life and death, were you not worried?” She said, “Life and death are allotted; I do not worry even for myself — why should I worry for you? It is only that people's words differ, and one cannot be certain how things stand; that is what makes one doubt.” We sat together in attendance, and toward dawn we made our final parting. My old mother charged me, “Take good care of yourself in the Way; do not worry about me. Now I too take my long farewell of you.” She set off on the road joyfully, without one backward look. I was moved that under heaven there are mothers such as this — does she not in one stroke exhaust all the feelings of birth and death? So I made this inscription for her, saying:

The love of mother and son: a lodestone drawing a needle. The wondrous nature is natural, perfect from the first. I see my mother as fire comes out of wood; the wood is burned away — the fire was never a self. Born, yet unattached; dying, as if unaware: only then do you see that this body of mine is the child of a stone maiden.
An Inscription on Clarifying the Mind, Shown to Ding Youwu

True nature is deep and still, like clear standing water. Love and hate strike it, and the waves of affliction rise. Rising without cease, the self-nature grows turbid; affliction and ignorance only deepen the unawareness. To grasp at the other with a self is like putting mud into water; to let the other stir me is like pouring oil on fire. The other troubles my truth, but the trouble is truly born of me. If I do not arise, the conflagration's burning turns to ice. Therefore the sage first empties the mark of self. If the mark of self is empty, from what can the other obstruct him? The work of forgetting the self lies in firm patience. The moment habit-energy stirs, suddenly give a sharp awakening; at the very place of awakening there is illumination — one thought turns the light back, sweeping away tracks and cutting off traces, and at once it is cool. Cool and still, standing alone, calm and joyful in spirit, nothing can stand against him.
An Inscription on Contemplating the Mind

Contemplate the body as no body — a mirror's image, the moon in water. Contemplate the mind as without marks — luminous and pure. When not one thought arises, it is empty, numinous, still and shining; perfect as the vast void, containing all wonders. It neither goes out nor comes in; it has no shape or feature. The hundred thousand skillful means all return to one pore. Do not rely on form and breath, for form and breath obstruct. Do not take deluded thought as real, for deluded thought breeds monstrosities. Contemplate this mind closely: it is hollow and empty, with nothing in it. In an instant feeling arises, and at once you feel dazed. At the critical moment turn the light back, and with all your strength shine upon it; the clouds scatter in the clear sky, and the white sun blazes. If the inner mind does not arise, outer objects are not born. Whatever has marks is not the original truth. When a thought arises, be aware; awareness at once shines through it. When an object comes, sweep it away; sweeping, let it go. The realms of good and evil transform with the mind; the forms of ordinary being and sage appear in response to thought. To hold mantras and contemplate the mind is like the medicine that polishes a mirror: once the dust and grime are gone, this too is not clung to. Vast and great spiritual powers are fully present in one's own mind; the Pure Land and the heavenly palaces — roam in them at will. You need not seek the truth: the mind itself is Buddha. If it is born in a place of heat, it ripens of itself in that place. Through the twelve hours of the day, everything is wondrous; wherever you touch, you are not deluded. This is called the essence of mind.
An Inscription on Mastering the Mind

Human nature is originally great, beyond form and vessel; it is only because there is a self that hindrances arise of themselves. When habits and defilements are thick, one is burdened by things; when learning is not broad, one is full of self-opinion. When principle is not clearly seen, one grows proud and leans on temper; one makes light of the inner and prizes the outer, chases things and loses the will. Cravings wound one's life, and one does not know what to avoid; one casts away oneself and forgets the truth — who would call this wisdom? The man of understanding keeps his heart empty, meets conditions without obstruction, yields with the times, plays in the world as dragon or snake. Gain and loss do not alarm him, high and low do not touch him; calm and tranquil, he gladdens his spirit, cutting thought short and stinting care. He strives at what he cannot yet do, is careful where he has not yet arrived; he learns non-doing, practices non-affairs, hears the unheard, sees the unseen. Turning back to look within, thought after thought he does not dwell; all delusions vanish, and the pure one is not two. This is the sage — the secret of mastering the mind. Seek it within yourself, and there is ample room; not to contemplate thus is called self-abandonment.
An Inscription on Awakening to One's Faults

A journey of ten thousand miles — every step is wrong; yet because the man is unaware, he does not shift an inch. A human life of a hundred years — thought after thought does not abide; the deluded press blindly on: who sorts the new from the old? Good and evil shift in turn, like a ring without an end; no one knows its limit, or who makes it so. The one who makes it does not know, and the newer it grows, the more deluded. The heels have nowhere to stand; lifting a foot brings weariness. When weariness has lasted long, one loses what one had; monstrosities come forth in hundreds, and one does not see their ugliness. Taking delusion for awakening, the whole earth goes astray; Momu apes a beauty's frown and is placidly pleased with herself. But let her come to the mirror for an instant and she will suddenly, sharply awaken: just still the mad mind — no need to apply powder. Natural beauty, brows and eyes clear and bright, the original face with not a hair's difference. Never mind fair or foul; no carving is needed. Leave it just as it is, and it returns to simplicity of itself. Awakening is not yes; unknowing is not knowing wrong. Spit out both right and wrong, and all things return as one.
An Inscription on Dream and Awakening

Good and evil have no beginning; it is one mind that turns and turns again. Sages and ordinary beings are not divided — only dream and awakening remain. To enter dream with awakening deepens the inversion; to enter awakening with dream brings liberation on the spot. Dream and awakening are both not it: still, numinous knowing, unborn and undying — what care, what thought? The hundred thousand illusions and transformations lie in a single thought. When a thought arises unawares, it is lightning in the vast void. If affliction does not knot, karma is not born. Love and hate, firm and hard, are truly the root of birth and death. Cause and effect, retribution, follow swift as shadow to form. If the root is not born, from what can the branches grow? Karma has many kinds, and killing stands first. All things love life and hate death — this is so for every one. Though the shells differ, the buddha-nature is the same. Only contemplate them equally, and the thought of killing empties itself. When the mind-mirror is buried in dust and habit is thick, wear it away with awakening, and the light will shine through of itself. As you grind, it falls away bit by bit; when a thought arises, be aware. When awareness reaches the unborn, mind and objects are empty and vast. Deluded thoughts racing after things are of no profit in the end. Examine and ponder this well: death and birth are swift. Birth and death come and go in a great, dark dream, turning only with karma — as if there were no birth. Born, yet unattached, one must wake from the dream. Seen with waking eyes, one binds oneself with no rope. Thought after thought, turn the light back; mind after mind, shine within. Simply do not follow feeling — this is called the essential wonder.
An Inscription on Forgetting Conditions

Feeling has wise and foolish; the nature has no brightness or dullness. The division between ordinary being and sage lies truly in turning toward or away. It is like a minister serving his lord, like a son attending his father: a single thought of pure truth allows no looking back or lingering. Linger, and it shifts; shift, and delusion is made. Once delusion has lasted long, the spirit grows weary day by day. Do not shift, and you awaken; awakened, you do not look back. Standing alone, deep and still, wondrous function ever abides. Responding to conditions like an echo, dwelling in the world like space, roaming free as things transform, in an instant you slip the cage. Neither going out nor coming in, no departing and no arriving. The world's marks are empty flowers; the breast holds the moon in water.
An Inscription on Contemplating the World

This illusory body of the four elements holds nothing at all; the foolish cling to it, shackled by love and hate. The wondrous, perfect, awakened mind is everywhere, pure and complete. Deluded thought piles up delusion, and inversion deepens the sickness. The thirsty deer chases the mirage: the more it chases, the thirstier it grows. See through it and rest — then you know it was a mistake. Playful spiritual powers never leave the daily round; high and low, fair and foul, let them tumble as they will. The man of understanding takes the great view and sees through it all: parting and meeting, sorrow and joy, are utterly unattainable. The realms of the six dusts are like treasures gathered in a dream; measureless greed and seeking end at a single awakening. Sound, voice, form, appearance — wind and moon moving through the sky: if you do not cling to them, are you blind and deaf? With this to meet the world, what hindrance can there be? The body is an ordinary being's, but the name is Avalokiteśvara, the Freely Contemplating Lord.
An Inscription on the Six Faculties

The body is the matchmaker of karma, the mind its seed. From the six roots of feeling come rushing greed and surging love. The eye flows out to forms and loses its true brightness; the ear flows out to sounds and loses its original hearing. The tongue misses no flavor, yet in truth it speaks many false words. Indulging will and feeling, the wind of consciousness stirs within; habit rises and the apertures hum, like a reed-pipe with a sound, no one knowing whence it comes, and the listener is shaken. Out of the mouth, into the ear — and love and hate arise. The sound has already died away, and the disaster is only beginning. Like thunder striking dung, suddenly poisonous fungi grow; the fool eats them and is accidentally killed. Nose and body together are one awareness — all are floating dust. The body has many faults and evils; the intellect is the pivot. Drifting on the waves of the poisonous sea, carried off by them, one muddles one's true lord. Therefore people in the world, though alive, are not alive. If you can look back, each faculty regains its pure truth. When the pure truth is restored, the six faculties hold nothing — like clouds floating in the sky, like an echo from the valley. Unbound by form, unhindered by mind, utterly beyond the dust of feeling, supremely at ease.
An Inscription on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation

Recite the Buddha, recite the mind; recite the mind, recite the Buddha. The Buddha is not outside the mind; the mind is not a thing. The self-nature is bright, mind after mind illumining. Deluded thoughts hide their tracks; the body is an empty valley. The Pure Land is never apart from what is before your eyes; lotuses ever line your two feet. Why wait for the life after this to be born there? Right here and now, neither going out nor coming in — this is precisely the Samādhi of Universal Light, and it lies in a single call from the man himself.
An Inscription on Rectifying the Mind

The mind is originally bright; obscured by desire, it grows dark. Its natural essence is dissipated as it follows feeling. To rectify it now, drive out desire and master feeling; once the one truth is restored, no delusion arises.
An Inscription on Making the Will Sincere
